newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says not worried by China-US military ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says not worried by China-US military ties.

text.p: Taiwan said on Wednesday it was not worried that warming U.S.-China military ties would harm the island's ability to procure advanced arms in the United States despite new Chinese pressure to halt such sales.

Taiwan Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling said he believed arms deals between Taipei and Washington would remain unchanged despite a U.S. visit by Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian seen as the latest sign of a thaw in frosty U.S.-China ties.
"We understand his (Chi's) itinerary and schedule. We know who he met," Chiang told a parliament committee meeting.
Chiang was unequivocal when asked by lawmakers whether Taipei expected Chi's U.S. visit would negatively affect access to advanced U.S. arms.
"There will not be any problem. I can promise," he said.

Washington severed ties with the exiled Republic of China on Taiwan to recognise China's communist government in 1979 but maintains a right to arm and even defend the Nationalist-ruled island that Beijing regards as a renegade province.

Chi, starting a fence-mending U.S. tour that was delayed by a year of squabbling, raised Beijing's concerns about Taiwan and its ongoing purchases of U.S. arms and pointedly refused to renounce its right to retake Taiwan by force if necessary.
Taiwan and China have been rivals since the Nationalist Chinese government lost a civil war to the communists in 1949 and fled into exile on the island.
In a blunt speech to U.S. military officers on Tuesday, Chi said the Beijing government would "not sit idly by" and allow Taiwan's leaders to continue "conniving" to split China.
Both Taipei and Beijing say they want to reunify, but refuse even to discuss their deep differences over how.

Worried that Taiwan's decade-old drive towards democracy has widened the gulf that divides them, Beijing launched months of war games and missile tests in waters off Taiwan in the run-up to the island's historic March 1996 presidential election.
In a dramatic gesture, Washington responded by dispatching two aircraft carrier groups to the region, the largest U.S. armada in the area since the Vietnam War.

The United States, which continued to recognise Taipei for eight years after it lost China's U.N. seat to Beijing in 1971, has resisted Chinese pressure to stop selling defensive arms to Taiwan -- unlike France and other western powers.

Two days before Chi's visit to Washington, the U.S. Army announced without elaboration that it had awarded a US$63 million contract to a Boeing Co unit to produce 74 high-tech Avenger anti-aircraft missile systems for Taiwan.
Taiwan also has been allowed to buy Patriot anti-missile missile batteries from U.S. defence giant Raytheon Co.
The Avengers and Patriots will enter service by 1999, boosting the island's defences against China's rapidly modernising People's Liberation Army.
